issues.legal_issue: Knowingly giving and clarifying a court undertaking that falsely implied the tenant remained in possession and could comply constitutes civil contempt.
material_facts: After an eviction decree was upheld, the tenant sought time to vacate and was granted time subject to an undertaking not to part with possession or create third-party interests.
The tenant gave the undertaking without disclosing that its chairman claimed to be a sub-tenant and had already sought to prevent execution of the eviction decree.

When challenged, the tenant’s counsel clarified that the undertaking meant the tenant was in possession; the Court found that the tenant and its chairman knew this implication was false and that the chairman was responsible for the undertaking and clarification.
The chairman’s claim to sub-tenancy and the parties’ conduct were found to be part of a course intended to delay or defeat execution of the eviction decree.
issues.conclusion: The tenant and its chairman committed civil contempt by knowingly giving the undertaking and instructing counsel to give a false clarification of its meaning.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, civil contempt includes wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court. Contempt proceedings are quasi-criminal, so the law must be strictly interpreted and its requirements strictly complied with. But knowingly giving an undertaking based on a false implication, and clarifying it falsely to mislead the court, establishes contempt. The Court relied on Noorali Babul Thanewala v. Sh. K.M.M. Shetty, which recognizes that breach of an undertaking given to a court on the faith of which it sanctions a course of action is misconduct amounting to contempt.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and court_undertaking_given and (undertaking_implied_present_possession or undertaking_implied_ability_to_comply) and responsible_persons_knew_implication_was_false and responsible_persons_authorized_false_clarification

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging civil contempt.
predicates.court_undertaking_given: A person or entity gave an undertaking to the court.
predicates.undertaking_implied_present_possession: The undertaking, as clarified or understood in context, represented that the person or entity remained in possession.
predicates.undertaking_implied_ability_to_comply: The undertaking, as clarified or understood in context, represented that the person or entity could comply with it.
predicates.responsible_persons_knew_implication_was: The persons responsible for giving the undertaking knew that its implication about possession or ability to comply was false.
predicates.responsible_persons_authorized_false_cla: The persons responsible for the undertaking authorized or consented to a clarification that they knew falsely described its meaning.

issues.definition: When a civil contempt proceeding concerns an undertaking that implies present possession or ability to comply, and the responsible persons knowingly give it a false meaning and authorize a false clarification, those persons commit civil contempt.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may use its power to do complete justice to secure a decree-holder’s possession pending determination of an unresolved competing sub-tenancy claim when interim orders are thwarting execution of an eviction decree.
material_facts: The landlord had obtained an eviction decree against the tenant.
The tenant’s chairman brought a declaratory suit claiming sub-tenancy and obtained an interim injunction that prevented execution of the decree.
The sub-tenancy claim had not been finally established, and the Court did not foreclose its determination in the declaratory suit.
The appeal was pending before the Supreme Court, which considered it unjust to allow the interim order to keep the decree-holder from possession while the claim remained unresolved.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the Court Receiver to take possession and appoint the decree-holder as agent in respect of the premises, notwithstanding interim orders from other courts, while leaving the claimant free to seek variation if he established his sub-tenancy right.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142(1) of the Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to make orders necessary to do complete justice in a matter before it. The Court may prevent parties from thwarting execution of an eviction decree while a competing sub-tenancy claim remains unestablished, without foreclosing that claim. Noorali Babul Thanewala v. Sh. K.M.M. Shetty supported the Court’s course of action concerning breach of an undertaking and the prevention of obstruction to relief.

rule.if: contempt_appeal_pending and eviction_decree_obtained and interim_order_blocks_execution and competing_subtenancy_claim_unresolved

predicates.contempt_appeal_pending: An appeal concerning contempt arising from conduct related to enforcement of a court decree was pending before the Supreme Court.
predicates.eviction_decree_obtained: A landlord had obtained an eviction decree against a tenant.
predicates.interim_order_blocks_execution: An interim order in another proceeding prevented execution of the eviction decree.
predicates.competing_subtenancy_claim_unresolved: A person’s competing claim to sub-tenancy had not been finally established.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerning contempt is pending, an eviction decree is obstructed by an interim order, and a competing sub-tenancy claim remains unresolved, the decree-holder receives possession pending determination of that claim.
